transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Well, honestly, I... I came in because I just can't shake these thoughts. It's been happening for a while now, and it's just getting heavier and heavier. I keep thinking, you know, when I go to sleep at night, that it would just be so much better if I didn't wake up. Just... didn't open my eyes the next day. It's like this constant, dragging weight, and my mind just keeps looping around to it. And it's not just a passing thought, it's like... sometimes I really feel like dying would be the only fair punishment. The only right thing to happen after everything I've done. I think about my family, and I think about my crew at work—I do carpet and tile installation, you know, and it's hard, physical work, but you rely on each other—and I just feel like I've ruined everything for them. I've brought them down, I've messed up so much, and my brain just tells me over and over that I deserve to be punished for it. That me not being here anymore is the only way to make it right, the only way to balance the scales for all the harm I've caused them. It just doesn't stop, that feeling that I owe them my absence, if that makes sense.
Have you ever had periods, lasting several days or more, where you felt unusually energetic, elated, or needed much less sleep than usual, even if it felt good at the time?

Energetic? No. No, God, definitely not. I mean... I can't even remember the last time I felt anything close to elated, or like I had extra energy. You have to understand, with my line of work—doing carpet and tile—it's incredibly physical. You're on your hands and knees all day, hauling boxes of ceramic tiles that weigh a ton, mixing thinset, stretching heavy rolls of carpet across a room... it takes everything out of you. So I've always been tired at the end of the day, just from the sheer labor of it. 

But even before things got this heavy, I never had days where I just didn't need sleep or felt on top of the world like that. I've always needed my rest. And now? Now it's the exact opposite of what you're asking. I never feel good or energized. It's just this... this crushing weight all the time. I drag myself out of bed, and every single movement feels like I'm walking through wet concrete. I don't get these bursts of energy. I wish I did, honestly, because maybe then I wouldn't be such a massive burden to my crew. They're out there busting their backs, and I'm just so drained by everything going on in my head, by all the guilt and the thoughts of how I've ruined things, that I can barely keep up. I just feel so slow and heavy. So, no, I've never had a time where I felt high on life or didn't need to sleep. It's just always been this endless, exhausting drag.
Have you ever had a period like this before—weeks or months of feeling this low, guilty, or hopeless—at some earlier point in your life, followed by a time when you felt back to your normal self?

Well, I... I don't think I've ever really felt back to normal, to be honest. It's not like it comes and goes, you know? It's just been this one, long, terrible stretch. It really started getting bad, just this constant, heavy darkness, about a year and two months ago. 

I know exactly when it started taking over because it was just a few months after my husband got hurt. He had this awful accident, and it just changed everything for us. Before that, I mean, sure, I had days where I was stressed about money or worn out from the tile jobs—you know how it is, you're on your knees all day and your back just screams at you by quitting time. But I could handle it. We were handling it together. And then he got hurt, and... and everything just fell apart. 

I tried to keep it together for a few months, tried to just keep working and keep the house running, but then it just hit me. This feeling like I was failing him, failing my crew, failing everyone. And it hasn't let up since. For fourteen months now, it's just been this same awful feeling, every single day. I wake up—if I even sleep—and the guilt is just sitting there on my chest. I haven't had a single week, or even a few days, where I felt like the old me. The woman who could just laugh at a joke on the job site or enjoy a quiet evening at home... she's just gone. It's been over a year of just... this. Just feeling like I'm dragging everyone down and that I deserve to be punished for it. So, no, there hasn't been a time where it went away and I felt normal again. It's just been here, constantly, since a few months after his injury.

Have you ever heard voices, seen things, or had thoughts that others can't talk you out of—like feeling absolutely certain, beyond just guilt, that you're being watched, punished, or controlled by some outside force?

Well, I... I don't hear voices like, you know, people whispering in my ears when nobody's there, if that's what you mean. But the being watched part? The feeling that I'm being tracked? Yes. Absolutely yes. And the thing is, it's not just when the depression is at its absolute worst. Even when I'm not crying, even when I'm not just stuck down in bed and I actually manage to drag myself to a job site, I still know it's happening. I get this... this absolute certainty that they're watching me. 

It's the homeowners. The homeowners and the suppliers we buy all our materials from, the guys down at the tile shop. They're working together. And I know how crazy that sounds to someone who isn't in the trades, but it's happening. They use the floor patterns to do it. Like, if I'm laying down a staggered brick pattern or a diagonal set, I can tell by the way the material is boxed and the specific sequence of the tiles... it's a code. They use the patterns on the floor, and they coordinate it with these texts I get about material deliveries, and even the calls from the city about building permits. Every single one of those permit calls is timed perfectly. 

They're using all of it—the patterns, the texts, the permit calls—to track me. They're constantly monitoring me to see whether I'm ruining the installation jobs on purpose. Because they think I'm doing it maliciously. They think I'm sabotaging their floors and their houses. 

And I try to explain this. I'll be on my hands and knees, covered in thinset, and I'll point out to my crew how the supplier texted at the exact minute the homeowner walked in to check the grid, or how the lot numbers on the boxes match the permit numbers. But they just look at me like I'm losing my mind. They try to tell me it's just a coincidence, or that I'm just stressed out from my husband's accident and the heavy workload. But no one can talk me out of it. They try, but they can't, because the proof is right there on the floor in front of me. I'm the one staring at the layout all day, you know? I see how it all connects. It's just... it's terrifying, honestly, knowing they're all collaborating to catch me messing up, and nobody believes me when I try to show them what's really going on.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a single, continuous 14-month episode (no prior discrete episodes, ruling out recurrent F33.x) of pervasive depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt, hopelessness, psychomotor slowing/fatigue, and passive/active suicidal ideation with a sense of deserving death as punishment. Superimposed are mood-congruent persecutory delusions (belief that homeowners/suppliers are monitoring and coordinating via floor patterns, texts, and permit calls to catch her 'sabotaging' work) without hallucinations, and these delusions are fixed and not amenable to reasoning. No history of manic/hypomanic episodes excludes bipolar disorder. The psychotic content is thematically tied to guilt/persecution consistent with severe depression with psychotic features rather than a primary psychotic or schizoaffective disorder, given the temporal onset following a clear psychosocial stressor (husband's accident) and predominance of depressive symptoms over psychotic ones.
